lessonTitle: Calcium and Metabolic Bone Disorders: Hypercalcaemia, Osteoporosis, Hypocalcaemia and Osteomalacia

blocks.text: A 72-year-old woman slips on a wet kitchen floor and fractures her wrist. She had a previous vertebral compression fracture two years ago, and no one tested her bones. Meanwhile, in the next bed, a man admitted with constipation, thirst and confusion has a calcium of 3.4 mmol/L. Calcium is tightly controlled, and which way it moves tells you where to look.

blocks.markdown: Plasma calcium is held within a narrow range (about 2.2 to 2.6 mmol/L total; ranges vary by laboratory) by **parathyroid hormone (PTH)**, **active vitamin D (calcitriol)** and, to a lesser extent, calcitonin. When calcium falls, the parathyroid glands release PTH, which raises calcium by increasing bone resorption, increasing renal calcium reabsorption and stimulating renal 1-alpha hydroxylation of vitamin D, thereby increasing gut absorption. PTH also lowers phosphate by increasing its renal excretion. About 40 to 45% of plasma calcium is bound to albumin, so measured calcium must be adjusted when albumin is abnormal.

blocks.caption: Albumin-adjusted calcium (a commonly used laboratory formula; many laboratories report an adjusted value).

blocks.title: Adjusting calcium for low albumin
blocks.prompt: A hospital patient has total calcium 2.05 mmol/L and albumin 25 g/L. Is she truly hypocalcaemic?

steps.text: Compute the albumin deficit from 40 g/L.
Multiply by 0.02 and add to the measured value.
2.35 mmol/L lies within the reference range. Low albumin lowers the total calcium but the physiologically active ionised fraction is normal.

blocks.answer: Adjusted calcium 2.35 mmol/L: normal, not true hypocalcaemia.

blocks.markdown: **Hypercalcaemia: ask what PTH is doing.** A high calcium should suppress PTH. If PTH is high or inappropriately normal, the parathyroid is the problem (**PTH-dependent**): primary hyperparathyroidism, usually from a single adenoma, with high calcium, low phosphate and often high PTH. If PTH is suppressed the cause is **PTH-independent**: malignancy (bone metastases, myeloma, or tumour secretion of PTH-related peptide), vitamin D excess, granulomatous disease such as sarcoidosis, thiazides, or thyrotoxicosis. Symptoms are summarised as bones (pain), stones (renal calculi), abdominal groans (constipation, pancreatitis) and psychic moans (low mood, confusion), plus polyuria and dehydration. Acute treatment of severe hypercalcaemia is IV fluids to correct dehydration, then an intravenous bisphosphonate (such as zoledronic acid) and treatment of the cause.

rows: Weight loss, smoker, rapidly rising calcium
blocks.caption: Calcium, PTH and phosphate patterns.

blocks.markdown: **Osteoporosis** is reduced bone mass and microarchitectural deterioration causing fragility fractures. Bone mineral density (BMD) is measured by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) and expressed as a **T-score**, the number of standard deviations from the mean of a healthy young adult. The WHO definition is: normal T-score of -1.0 or above; osteopenia between -1.0 and -2.5; osteoporosis -2.5 or below. A fragility fracture (a fracture from a fall from standing height or less) strongly suggests osteoporosis in itself. Risk is assessed by tools such as FRAX or QFracture, combining age, sex, previous fracture, parental hip fracture, smoking, alcohol, glucocorticoid use, rheumatoid arthritis and (optionally) BMD, to estimate a 10-year probability of fracture. Treatment is by lifestyle, adequate calcium and vitamin D, and an oral bisphosphonate (such as alendronic acid) first line, with other agents when bisphosphonates are not suitable. Vitamin D deficiency and hypocalcaemia must be corrected first.

blocks.title: Calculating a T-score
blocks.prompt: A woman's lumbar spine BMD is 0.74 g/cm2. The young adult mean is 1.00 g/cm2 with a standard deviation of 0.12 g/cm2. Classify the result.

steps.text: -2.17 lies between -1.0 and -2.5, so by WHO criteria this is osteopenia, not osteoporosis.
Fracture risk is still estimated with a tool such as FRAX, because a prior fragility fracture or glucocorticoid use could justify treatment regardless.

blocks.answer: T-score -2.17: osteopenia; assess fracture risk before deciding on treatment.

items: Hypocalcaemia causes perioral and fingertip paraesthesia, muscle cramps, tetany, carpopedal spasm, seizures and a prolonged QT interval. Chvostek and Trousseau signs are classic examination findings.
Causes include hypoparathyroidism (for example after thyroid surgery), vitamin D deficiency, chronic kidney disease, hypomagnesaemia and acute pancreatitis.
Severe or symptomatic hypocalcaemia: intravenous calcium gluconate (teaching example: 10 mL of 10% over 10 minutes with ECG monitoring), then an infusion; correct magnesium; treat the cause.

Osteomalacia (adult rickets) is defective mineralisation of bone from vitamin D deficiency: bone pain, proximal myopathy, low or normal calcium, low phosphate, raised alkaline phosphatase, raised PTH, low 25-OH vitamin D, and Looser zones (pseudofractures) on X-ray.
Treatment of osteomalacia is vitamin D (colecalciferol) loading then maintenance, with calcium, and treating any underlying malabsorption or renal cause.

blocks.title: Before you start a bisphosphonate
blocks.text: Check calcium, vitamin D, renal function and dental health. A bisphosphonate given to a patient who is vitamin D deficient can cause symptomatic hypocalcaemia, and unrecognised osteomalacia will not respond to it.

points: Calcium is controlled by PTH and vitamin D; always adjust calcium for albumin.
Hypercalcaemia: high or inappropriately normal PTH means primary hyperparathyroidism; suppressed PTH means malignancy, vitamin D excess or granulomatous disease.
Osteoporosis is diagnosed by T-score of -2.5 or below or by fragility fracture; treatment is guided by fracture risk (for example FRAX).
Symptomatic hypocalcaemia needs IV calcium gluconate with ECG monitoring; osteomalacia is treated with vitamin D and calcium.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with recurrent renal stones has adjusted calcium 2.95 mmol/L, phosphate 0.65 mmol/L (low) and PTH 9.5 pmol/L (raised). What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Secondary hyperparathyroidism from chronic kidney disease

distractorRationale.a: Correct: high calcium with raised PTH and low phosphate.
distractorRationale.c: Vitamin D toxicity suppresses PTH and raises phosphate.
distractorRationale.d: Secondary hyperparathyroidism has low or normal calcium and high phosphate.

questions.explanation: A raised calcium should suppress PTH, so a raised PTH means the parathyroid is autonomous. PTH lowers phosphate by increasing renal excretion and promotes stones through hypercalciuria.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old smoker with weight loss and haemoptysis has adjusted calcium 3.4 mmol/L, suppressed PTH and low phosphate. What is the most likely mechanism of the hypercalcaemia?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: PTH is suppressed and malignancy is likely.
distractorRationale.b: An adenoma would give a high or inappropriately normal PTH.
distractorRationale.c: Thiazides cause mild hypercalcaemia and would not explain the picture.

questions.explanation: A suppressed PTH means the hypercalcaemia is not parathyroid driven. In a smoker with weight loss, a lung tumour secreting PTH-related peptide (or bone metastases) is the likely cause.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman has a DXA lumbar spine T-score of -2.8. Using WHO criteria, what does this indicate?

distractorRationale.d: Osteomalacia is a mineralisation disorder, diagnosed biochemically, not by T-score.

questions.explanation: The WHO definition of osteoporosis is a T-score of -2.5 or lower. A T-score of -2.8 meets that, so fracture risk assessment and treatment should be considered.

questions.stem: Two days after a total thyroidectomy a woman has perioral tingling and carpopedal spasm, with adjusted calcium 1.65 mmol/L and a prolonged QT interval. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Intravenous calcium gluconate with ECG monitoring

questions.correctOptionText: Intravenous calcium gluconate with ECG monitoring

distractorRationale.a: Correct: symptomatic hypocalcaemia with ECG change needs IV calcium.
distractorRationale.b: Vitamin D takes days to act and is not the emergency treatment.
distractorRationale.c: Bisphosphonates lower calcium and would worsen the problem.

questions.explanation: Hypoparathyroidism after thyroid surgery causes acute hypocalcaemia, with neuromuscular excitability and QT prolongation that can precipitate arrhythmia or seizures. Intravenous calcium gluconate acts immediately and is followed by maintenance therapy and vitamin D.

questions.stem: Which biochemical pattern is most typical of osteomalacia due to dietary vitamin D deficiency?

options.text: Low 25-OH vitamin D, low or normal calcium, low phosphate, raised alkaline phosphatase and raised PTH
High calcium, low PTH, normal alkaline phosphatase
Normal calcium, phosphate and ALP with low T-score
High calcium, high PTH, low phosphate

questions.correctOptionText: Low 25-OH vitamin D, low or normal calcium, low phosphate, raised alkaline phosphatase and raised PTH

distractorRationale.a: Correct: defective mineralisation with secondary hyperparathyroidism.
distractorRationale.c: This is the usual biochemistry of osteoporosis.

questions.explanation: Without vitamin D, gut calcium absorption falls, PTH rises and phosphate is lost in urine, while osteoblast activity increases alkaline phosphatase. The result is soft, poorly mineralised bone with pain and proximal weakness.

questions.stem: A patient has a total calcium of 2.90 mmol/L and albumin 28 g/L. Using the adjustment of 0.02 mmol/L per 1 g/L that albumin is below 40 g/L, calculate the albumin-adjusted calcium in mmol/L.
questions.explanation: Adjusted calcium = 2.90 + 0.02 x (40 - 28) = 2.90 + 0.24 = 3.14 mmol/L. This is clearly raised, so low albumin has been hiding the true degree of hypercalcaemia and the PTH should be measured.

questions.stem: A woman's femoral neck BMD is 0.62 g/cm2. The young adult mean is 0.93 g/cm2 and the standard deviation is 0.12 g/cm2. Calculate her T-score (unitless).
questions.explanation: T = (0.62 - 0.93) / 0.12 = -2.58. This is below -2.5, so by WHO criteria she has osteoporosis.

questions.stem: Describe how you would investigate and classify a patient with hypercalcaemia (adjusted calcium 3.0 mmol/L), using PTH to separate causes.
markingGuide: Confirm with albumin-adjusted calcium and repeat
High or inappropriately normal PTH: primary hyperparathyroidism (PTH-dependent)
PTH-independent examples: malignancy (PTHrP, bone metastases, myeloma), vitamin D excess, sarcoidosis, thiazides, thyrotoxicosis
Further tests: phosphate, vitamin D, renal function, urinary calcium, imaging or myeloma screen as indicated
Acute severe: IV fluids then bisphosphonate
questions.explanation: Raised calcium normally suppresses PTH, so PTH tells you whether the parathyroid is behaving autonomously or whether another process is raising calcium. This single result divides the differential and directs imaging, vitamin D measurement or a search for malignancy.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old woman has had a hip fracture after a fall from standing height. Outline the diagnostic and fracture-risk approach to osteoporosis, and the principles of first-line treatment.
markingGuide: DXA with T-score; -2.5 or below is osteoporosis
Risk factors: age, previous fracture, parental hip fracture, smoking, alcohol, glucocorticoids, rheumatoid arthritis
Risk tools such as FRAX or QFracture estimate 10-year fracture probability
Exclude secondary causes and check calcium, vitamin D and renal function
Treatment: calcium and vitamin D, oral bisphosphonate first line
Correct vitamin D deficiency or hypocalcaemia before bisphosphonate
questions.explanation: A fragility fracture marks a skeleton that is already unable to bear normal loads, so risk is judged by fracture history and risk factors as well as by T-score. Bisphosphonates reduce resorption but depend on adequate calcium and vitamin D.

questions.stem: True or false: vitamin D deficiency and hypocalcaemia should be corrected before starting a bisphosphonate for osteoporosis.
questions.explanation: Bisphosphonates reduce bone resorption and can lower serum calcium, so in a vitamin D deficient patient they may precipitate symptomatic hypocalcaemia. Vitamin D deficiency may also mean osteomalacia, which would not respond to bisphosphonate treatment.
